title: WHY PAUL SHOOK THE SNAKE INTO THE FIRE
paragraphs:
WHY PAUL SHOOK THE SNAKE INTO THE FIRE
The serpent expected Paul to die. The people expected judgment. But God was writing a completely different ending—and what Paul did next may expose the venom you have been carrying far too long.
There are moments when life does not even give you time to recover before something else bites you.
Paul had just survived a shipwreck.
Think about that.
The storm had already been violent enough.
The ship was gone.
The cargo was gone.
The soldiers had considered killing the prisoners.
The sea had nearly swallowed everyone alive.
Paul finally crawled onto the shore of Malta soaked, exhausted, cold, and probably carrying the physical consequences of fourteen terrifying days at sea.
And then, while he was simply trying to help build a fire…
a snake fastened itself to his hand.
Somebody reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
Not literally.
But spiritually.
Emotionally.
You survived one thing only to be bitten by another.
You survived the betrayal, then came the financial problem.
You survived the funeral, then came the family conflict.
You survived the addiction, then temptation returned.
You survived the breakup, but bitterness followed you onto the shore.
You survived the season that almost destroyed your faith, and just when you thought you could finally warm yourself beside the fire…
something came out of the wood.
That is where Acts 28 becomes painfully personal.
Luke writes:
Acts 28:3
The Greek is even more vivid.
The creature is called an ἔχιδνα—echidna—a viper or venomous snake.
And Luke says it καθῆψε τῆς χειρὸς αὐτοῦ—kathēpse tēs cheiros autou.
It fastened onto his hand.
It did not merely appear near Paul.
It attached itself to him.
And sometimes that is the difference between a problem and a wound.
Some things happen around you.
Other things fasten themselves to you.
A betrayal happens…
then distrust fastens itself to you.
Abuse happens…
then shame fastens itself to you.
Failure happens…
then the sentence “I will never be enough” fastens itself to you.
Someone abandons you…
then fear of abandonment starts following you into every relationship.
You commit a sin you deeply regret…
Christ offers forgiveness, yet condemnation still hangs from your hand years later.
The event may have lasted minutes.
The venom can remain in your thinking for decades.
And here is what makes the scene even more brutal.
People were watching.
Acts tells us that when the islanders saw the creature hanging from Paul’s hand, they immediately began interpreting his suffering.
They said:
“No doubt this man is a murderer. Though he has escaped from the sea, Justice has not allowed him to live.”
Acts 28:4
Paul had not even collapsed…
and people had already written his obituary.
They saw the snake and assumed they understood the man.
They saw suffering and called it guilt.
They saw circumstances and constructed a theology around them.

The word translated “Justice” is Δίκη—Dikē—which in the Greco-Roman world could refer to divine justice and was also personified as a goddess. The islanders were interpreting Paul’s circumstances through their own worldview.
The sea did not kill him?
Then surely divine justice sent the snake.
Case closed.
Except they were completely wrong.
And that should humble every Christian who has ever looked at another person’s suffering and quietly decided,
“I know why God allowed this.”
Sometimes you do not.
Job’s friends made that mistake.
They looked at suffering and assumed hidden wickedness.
Jesus confronted similar thinking when His disciples encountered the man born blind and asked:
“Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?”
Jesus answered:
“It was not that this man sinned, or his parents, but that the works of God might be displayed in him.”
John 9:2–3
Be careful when you interpret somebody else’s storm.
Be careful when you interpret somebody else’s snake.
And be especially careful when you interpret your own suffering as proof that God has abandoned you.
Paul was bitten.
But Paul was not abandoned.
That distinction could save someone’s faith tonight.
The presence of pain is not proof of the absence of God.
Paul was exactly where God’s providence had brought him, yet there was still a storm.
There was still a shipwreck.
There was still cold.
There was still a snake.
Biblical Christianity never promises that obedience makes Christians untouchable.
Jesus Himself said:
“In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world.”
John 16:33
Christian faith is not the promise that nothing painful will ever fasten itself to your hand.
It is the confidence that nothing can ultimately separate those who belong to Christ from the love of God.
And then Paul does something astonishing.
Acts 28:5 says:
“He, however, shook off the creature into the fire and suffered no harm.”
The Greek expression is beautifully forceful:
ὁ μὲν οὖν ἀποτινάξας τὸ θηρίον εἰς τὸ πῦρ…
ho men oun apotinaxas to thērion eis to pyr…
He shook the creature off…
into the fire.
The verb ἀποτινάσσω—apotinassō—carries the idea of shaking something off.
Paul did not negotiate with the snake.
He did not study the snake.
He did not carry the snake around as evidence of how difficult his journey had been.
He did not make the snake his identity.
He shook it off.
Now hear this carefully, because Acts 28 should not be turned into a motivational slogan that ignores what the passage actually says.
Luke is describing a historical event.

This passage is not permission for Christians to handle venomous snakes, deliberately expose themselves to danger, refuse appropriate medical care, or presume that God must miraculously protect them from physical harm.
Paul did not pick up the snake to prove his faith.
The snake unexpectedly attacked him.
The miracle was God’s sovereign protection, not Paul performing a religious stunt.
But there is still a powerful truth in the way Paul responded.
What attached itself to Paul did not become Paul.
And what happened to you does not have to become your identity either.
Read that again.
What attached itself to Paul did not become Paul.
You may have been betrayed.
You are not betrayal.
You may have failed.
You are not your failure.
You may have sinned terribly.
Your sin is serious—but if you have come to Jesus Christ in genuine repentance and faith, your sin does not have the authority to write the final chapter of your life.
You may have been abused.
What somebody did to you does not define your worth.
You may have gone through divorce.
You may have gone through bankruptcy.
You may have gone through addiction.
You may have buried somebody you thought would grow old beside you.
You may have disappointed people.
You may have disappointed yourself.
You may even be reading this while secretly carrying something nobody on Facebook knows.
But the Gospel announces something scandalously beautiful:
Jesus Christ is greater than the worst chapter of your story.
That does not mean consequences magically disappear.
It does not mean trauma becomes imaginary.
It does not mean repentance is unnecessary.
It means your past does not possess greater authority than the cross.
This is where Christianity separates itself from cheap inspiration.
The Gospel does not tell sinful people,
“You were perfect all along.”
Scripture says something infinitely more powerful.
We have sinned.
“All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.”
Romans 3:23
Sin is real.
Judgment is real.
Our guilt before a holy God is real.
And therefore our greatest problem is deeper than bad circumstances, difficult people, trauma, disappointment, or snakes emerging from fires.
We need reconciliation with God.
And this is where Jesus enters the story.
Not merely as an inspirational teacher.
Not merely as an example.
Not merely as someone who helps good people become slightly better.
Christ came for sinners.
Paul himself would write:
Romans 5:8
At the cross, Jesus bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
The Gospel is not God pretending your sin never mattered.
The Gospel is God demonstrating how much sin mattered by giving His Son—and demonstrating how enormous His grace is by offering forgiveness to people who could never purchase it themselves.
That is scandalous grace.
The guilty can be forgiven.
The ashamed can be cleansed.
The rebel can come home.
The addict can repent.
The sexually broken can be restored.
The liar can become truthful.
The proud can bow.
The religious hypocrite can finally stop pretending.
The person everybody gave up on can become evidence that Jesus Christ still saves sinners.
From scandal…
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And perhaps the snake hanging from your hand right now is not something somebody did to you.
Perhaps it is something you did.
That is harder to admit.
Maybe you have been blaming your childhood for something God has been telling you to repent of.
Maybe pornography has fastened itself to your private life.
Maybe resentment has become so normal that you call it discernment.
Maybe pride has learned Christian vocabulary.
Maybe jealousy hides behind criticism.
Maybe you worship God publicly while feeding something privately that is slowly poisoning your marriage, your mind, your integrity, or your relationship with Christ.
Maybe everybody sees the fire…
but only you know about the snake.
Do not merely manage what Christ is calling you to surrender.
Shake it off.
Not through willpower alone.
Not through positive thinking.
Not by pretending temptation does not exist.
Bring it into the light.
Confess it.
Repent.
Seek accountability.
Remove access to what repeatedly leads you into sin.
Ask mature believers for help.
And run to Christ.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
1 John 1:9
Notice where Paul threw the snake.
Into the fire.
There are things you should not keep souvenirs from.
Some doors need to stay closed.
Some numbers need to remain deleted.
Some conversations need to end.
Some secret accounts need to disappear.
Some environments need to be abandoned.
Some relationships require biblical boundaries.
Some habits need more than another emotional promise that “this was the last time.”
Repentance is not merely feeling terrible about what happened.
The New Testament word μετάνοια—metanoia—speaks of repentance, a genuine turning of mind and direction toward God.
Grace does not teach us to cuddle the snake.
Grace teaches us to leave the old master and belong to Christ.
But there is another detail in Acts 28 that many people rush past.
The people were waiting for Paul to die.
Acts 28:6 says they expected him to swell up or suddenly fall down dead.
Imagine the silence.
Everyone staring.
Waiting.
Watching.
Perhaps you know that feeling too.
Some people remember the old you so clearly that they cannot imagine anything else.
They remember your addiction.
Your divorce.
Your scandal.
Your prison sentence.
Your breakdown.
Your affair.
Your bankruptcy.
Your anger.
Your rebellion.
Your years away from God.
Your worst decision.
And sometimes you can almost feel people waiting for you to become that person again.
Paul simply kept standing.
Eventually, the observers changed their minds dramatically and wrongly concluded that he was a god.
First murderer.
Then god.
Same Paul.
Different public opinion.
That should teach you something.
If you build your identity from what people say about you, you will spend your entire life being emotionally dragged between condemnation and worship.
One crowd will call you worthless.
Another will call you extraordinary.
Neither crowd gets the final word.
God does.
Paul knew who he belonged to.
Earlier, during the storm, he had said:
“the God to whom I belong and whom I worship.”
Acts 27:23
That was Paul’s anchor.
Not public opinion.
Not the snake.
Not the storm.
Not Rome.
Not Malta.
Not his chains.
“I belong to God.”
There is somebody reading these words who desperately needs to recover that sentence.
If you are in Christ…
you belong to Him.
Your scandal does not own you.
Your shame does not own you.
Your addiction does not own you.
Your critics do not own you.
Your trauma does not own you.
Your achievements do not own you.
Jesus Christ purchased His people at immeasurable cost.
And perhaps that is why the enemy of your soul has worked so relentlessly to convince you that your worst moment is your permanent name.
Because shame whispers,
“Hide.”
Jesus says,
“Come.”
Shame says,
“You are too dirty.”
Jesus cleanses sinners.
Shame says,
“If people knew everything, nobody could love you.”
The cross says God already knows the depth of human sin—and Christ still came.
Shame says,
“Your story ended there.”
The resurrection says death itself does not get the final word.
That is why the Gospel is not self-improvement.
It is resurrection.
And something remarkable happens after Paul survives the snake.
The story keeps moving.

Paul later ministers on Malta. Publius receives him. Publius’s father is sick with fever and dysentery. Paul prays, lays his hands on him, and the man is healed. Others on the island who were sick also come and receive healing.
The hand that had just carried a snake becomes a hand laid upon a suffering man in prayer.
Do not miss that.
The wounded hand became a serving hand.
The hand everybody expected to become swollen and useless was soon being used in ministry.
God can do something beautiful with the places where you thought your story was finished.
Again, we must be biblically careful: Acts 28 does not promise that every believer will experience miraculous physical healing or supernatural protection in exactly the same manner as Paul.
But it unmistakably shows the sovereignty of God working through circumstances that looked catastrophic.
The shipwreck did not stop the mission.
The snake did not stop the mission.
The opinions of the crowd did not stop the mission.
And eventually Paul continued toward Rome.
What looked like interruption was still inside providence.
Maybe you have spent years asking,
“God, why did You allow this?”
Some questions may not receive complete answers in this life.
Christianity does not require us to pretend otherwise.
But Scripture repeatedly reveals a God who can accomplish His purposes even through suffering without calling evil good.
Joseph could look backward at the cruelty committed against him and say:
“You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good.”
Genesis 50:20
Not that evil secretly became good.
It was evil.
But evil did not outrank God.
The cross itself is the ultimate demonstration.
Human beings committed the greatest injustice in history against the sinless Son of God.
Yet through that very cross, according to God’s sovereign purpose, redemption came.
Then the tomb was opened.
That means Christians do not need to pretend their scars never happened.
We point to the scars and say:
“Jesus met me there.”
You survived the sea.
Then came the snake.
But perhaps you are still here because the story is not finished.
Perhaps your testimony will not be,
“Nothing painful ever happened to me.”
Perhaps it will be,
“It happened. It hurt. I cried. I stumbled. I needed help. There were nights I questioned everything. But Jesus Christ did not abandon me.”
That testimony has weight.
Because somebody else is still floating in the wreckage you once escaped.
Somebody else is staring at the same addiction.
Somebody else is hiding the same shame.
Somebody else is sitting inside a parked car crying before walking into the house because nobody there knows how exhausted they really are.
Somebody else opened Facebook tonight because silence felt unbearable.
And somehow…
they found this.
Maybe you did too.
What is still hanging from my hand that Jesus is calling me to stop carrying?
Bitterness?
Pornography?
Unforgiveness?
Pride?
Secret sin?
Condemnation?
Fear?
A relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ?
A version of yourself God has been calling you to bury?
You do not need to tell strangers every detail.
But you do need to stop hiding from God.
He already knows.
Come to Jesus.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Receive the forgiveness purchased by Christ rather than trying to manufacture your own righteousness.
And if you already belong to Him but you have wandered…
come home.
There is still grace.
Not because typing words saves you.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes confession begins when somebody finally stops pretending.
Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded person desperately needed tonight.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
Not because an algorithm can advance the Kingdom of God by itself.
But because somebody in your circle may be quietly drowning while looking perfectly fine in photographs.
If Christ has used these words to strengthen you, sharing Gospel-centered truth is one practical way you can help place that truth in front of someone who might never search for it themselves.
Because there may come a night when the snake returns to your memory and you need to remember:
what fastened itself to you does not have to define you.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend who stopped attending church.
Invite the believer who is tired.
Invite the person who has questions.
Invite the person everybody else has written off.
Invite even the unbeliever who thinks Christianity has nothing to say to broken people.
Because Christianity begins with the astonishing announcement that Christ came precisely because humanity is broken by sin—and sinners can be reconciled to God through Him.
But supporting Gospel work can be a practical expression of generosity and partnership when done freely, prayerfully, and with the right heart.
Leave changed.
Because Paul shaking a snake into a fire is fascinating.
But the greater story is not about Paul being powerful.
It is about God being faithful.
Paul was not the hero of Christianity.
Jesus is.
Paul eventually died.
Every miracle in Acts points beyond the messenger toward the God who reigns over life and death.
And the greatest victory promised to Christians is not that every snake will fail to bite.
It is not that every storm will disappear.
It is not that every sickness will be healed before death.
It is not that everybody who misunderstood you will eventually apologize.
Our hope is greater.
Jesus Christ was crucified.
Jesus Christ was buried.
Jesus Christ rose from the dead.
And everyone who turns from sin and trusts in Him has a hope no storm, accusation, failure, grave, devil, or serpent can ultimately destroy.
So perhaps tonight is your fire.
Perhaps tonight is where you finally stop carrying what should have been surrendered years ago.
Let the bitterness fall.
Let the secret life come into the light.
Let the shame lose its throne.
Let repentance become more than a word.
Let grace become more than a doctrine you quote for other people.
Come to Christ yourself.
The snake may explain part of what happened to you.
It does not get to write the ending.
The storm may explain why you are tired.
It does not get to name you.
Your scandal may explain yesterday.
It does not possess tomorrow.

Because when Jesus Christ takes hold of a surrendered life, even the chapter you thought would permanently disqualify you can become the place where somebody else discovers what grace actually looks like.
And maybe the most powerful thing you will ever do with the thing that tried to poison your future…
is finally stop carrying it.
Shake it into the fire.
Then keep walking with Jesus.
The venom may have touched your story—but it does not get to hold the pen.
